title: Blitz: Accelerating the Diffusion Modulesof AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2

paper.title: Blitz: Accelerating the Diffusion Modules of AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion-based atom prediction has been a major breakthrough in the biological sciences, with models such as AlphaFold3 ( Abramson et al., 2024 ) , Boltz-1 and Boltz-2 ( Wohlwend et al., 2024 ; Passaro et al., 2025 ) , Chai-1 ( Chai Discovery et al., 2024 ) , and Protenix ( ByteDance AML AI4Science Team et al., 2025 ) . It builds on progress in protein folding that led CASP organizers to describe AlphaFold2 as a solution to the decades-old folding problem for single protein chains ( Abbass, 2025 ) . However, these models are expensive in pipelines that require tens of thousands of predictions, leading to a growing literature on reducing their cost. These efforts primarily tackle three parts of the pipeline: 1. Reducing the cost of constructing multiple sequence alignments (MSAs). MMseqs2 and ColabFold accelerate sequence search ( Steinegger & Söding, 2017 ; Mirdita et al., 2022 ) , while Kallenborn et al. (2025) move the search onto GPUs. 2. Reducing the number of recycle updates and the computational cost of the Pairformer trunk ( Gong et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . 3. Reducing the cost of the diffusion model itself, which typically uses 200 denoising steps in AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 ( Abramson et al., 2024 ; Passaro et al., 2025 ) . On the model side, these costs have been approached in several ways. Gong et al. (2025) introduced Protenix-Mini, reducing both the cost of the trunk and the number of diffusion sampling steps. Zhang et al. (2026) introduced DCFold, whose Temporal Geodesic Matching schedule pairs diffusion times during consistency training to improve stability. They also apply consistency training to the Pairformer to reduce recycling. Scarpellini et al. (2026) introduced DeCAF, which distills all-atom flow maps in the noise coordinate used by EDM and applies reward-guided search at inference. They report strong results in both protein–ligand pose accuracy and physical validity. However, we show here that differences in scoring conventions and benchmark construction make these algorithms difficult to compare. Claims of preserved quality do not fully hold under our unified evaluation. This is especially important for few-step samplers, where steric clashes, distorted bonds, and invalid bond angles can coexist with high structural similarity scores. Our matched evaluations show that commonly reported accuracy metrics can obscure these flaws when stereochemical checks are omitted (Table 1 and Figure 1 ). To address these gaps in stereochemical quality and structural accuracy, we present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework. We first show that the default polynomial noise schedule of Karras et al. (2022) is ill-suited to the few-step molecular sampling regime studied here, and replace it with a geometric schedule. We then address the remaining accuracy gap with multistep consistency training on this grid, adapting the method of Heek et al. (2024) . The eight-step trajectory also leaves room for inference-time steering, as used in Boltz-2 ( Passaro et al., 2025 ) . We tune the steering strengths for Boltz-2-Blitz and bring its reference-free validity closer to that of its teacher. Finally, we benchmark structural accuracy and stereochemical quality on three popular datasets used in this literature: the Boltz-2 benchmark ( ∼ \sim 2,300 targets), Runs N’ Poses, and RecentPDB384 ( Passaro et al., 2025 ; Škrinjar et al., 2025 ; ByteDance AML AI4Science Team et al., 2025 ) . Among the compared configurations, AF3-Blitz achieves the highest stereochecked complex lDDT on the primary benchmark. Both students retain teacher-level structural accuracy, exceeding their teachers on several reported metrics. We apply the same framework to AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 to show generality across two publicly available diffusion-based structure prediction models. In summary, our core contributions are: 1. A diagnosis. We show that prevailing scoring and benchmark conventions systematically mask the geometric failures of few-step structure predictors, and we expose these failures under matched evaluation. 2. A method. We introduce Blitz, which pairs a geometric noise schedule and multistep consistency training with inference-time physical controls to reach teacher-level structural accuracy in eight sampling steps, a 25 × 25\times reduction in sampling steps for both AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2. 3. A protocol. We establish a standardized, multi-metric evaluation across three benchmarks spanning structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemistry, designed to surface the failure modes that single-metric reporting hides.

sections.text: AF3 adopts the EDM formulation and polynomial noise schedule of Karras et al. Its diffusion module is a non-equivariant transformer conditioned on the single and pair representations from the trunk. sections.heading: Consistency models.
sections.text: Consistency models learn to map points on the same probability-flow trajectory to its low-noise endpoint ( Song et al., 2023 ) . For two states x s , x t x_{s},x_{t} on that trajectory, the desired property is f θ ​ ( x s , s ) = f θ ​ ( x t , t ) f_{\theta}(x_{s},s)=f_{\theta}(x_{t},t) , with the boundary condition f θ ​ ( x ε , ε ) = x ε f_{\theta}(x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon)=x_{\varepsilon} at a small positive endpoint ε \varepsilon . In consistency distillation, a frozen diffusion teacher takes a numerical step to form a pair of nearby states. Training brings their student predictions together, stopping gradients through the target branch. Consistency training instead forms pairs directly from noised data, without a pretrained teacher ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Multistep consistency models.
sections.text: Heek et al. (2024) unify TRACT ( Berthelot et al., 2023 ) and consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) by dividing the trajectory into fixed segments. A shared model maps each point to the lower boundary of its segment. Generation traverses the segments in order, using one evaluation per segment. Their formulation uses variance-preserving coordinates, z t = α t ​ x 0 + β t ​ ϵ , α t 2 + β t 2 = 1 , z_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\beta_{t}\epsilon,\qquad\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}=1, (3) and constructs the segment maps with DDIM updates.

sections.heading: 3 What does it mean to preserve quality in structure prediction?
sections.text: The prediction in Figure 1 a has severe overlap between its protein chains. Despite having recognizable individual folds, this arrangement is sterically implausible; however, it still scores well on unchecked lDDT. Its Boltz-1x teacher, shown in Figure 1 b, retains recognizable folds without this severe overlap; this raises an important question: what must accelerated structure prediction preserve when we remove these denoising steps? This is particularly important when there is a claim that a faster sampler preserves accuracy. Unchecked lDDT measures how well local interatomic distances are preserved from the reference. However, this local fold preservation can coexist with severe clashes and violations of bond lengths and angles. The original lDDT authors anticipated this distinction and provided optional stereochemical checks to account for these violations ( Mariani et al., 2013 ) . PoseBusters showed that agreement with an experimental ligand pose does not necessarily establish physical plausibility ( Buttenschoen et al., 2024 ) . However, evaluations like those done by DCFold report only RMSD thresholds on the PoseBusters benchmark without reporting PB-validity, leaving the failure mode that motivated those checks unexamined ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . This concern also applies to cofolding. AlphaFold3 documents overlapping chains ( Abramson et al., 2024 ) , and DeCAF reports ligand validity alongside pose accuracy ( Scarpellini et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1 helps illustrate the discrepancy at the protein-assembly level. Figure 1: Selected 8V9Q example ( Collette et al., 2024 ) : experimental reference, (a) released DeCAF, and (b) its Boltz-1x teacher. Scores show lDDT without → \to with stereochemical checks. Table 1 helps make this discrepancy in the evaluated configurations more explicit. On matched targets from the Boltz-2 benchmark ( ∼ \sim 2,300 targets), the default Protenix sampler and its one-step ODE counterpart are almost identical on unchecked lDDT. DCFold uses a corresponding Protenix-based one-step ODE configuration as its untrained AF3 ODE baseline ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . However, with stereochemical checks enabled, our one-step configuration’s score falls approximately 32 points on a 100-point scale, while the default sampler’s score changes only slightly. Furthermore, the one-step configuration has, on average, approximately 1,500 counted bond-length, bond-angle, and clash violations per target. sections.heading: 4.1 Noise allocation before distillation
sections.text: Before detailing our distillation procedure, we identify a problem with the noise schedule in the low-step regime. Following the deterministic analysis of Karras et al. (2022) , we hold the pretrained AF3 denoiser and solver fixed and replace the default Karras schedule with a geometric schedule. Stereochemically checked lDDT improves while bond violations and clashes decrease, as shown in Figure 2 . Critically, the improvement is largest at the smallest step budgets. The same pattern holds across every publicly available structure generation model we evaluated. The geometric schedule is the ρ → ∞ \rho\to\infty limit of Equation 2 : σ i = σ max 1 − u i σ min u i , u i = i K − 1 , i = 0 , … , K − 1 . \sigma_{i}=\sigma_{\max}^{1-u_{i}}\sigma_{\min}^{u_{i}},\qquad u_{i}=\frac{i}{K-1},\quad i=0,\ldots,K-1. (4) It spaces the positive nodes uniformly in log noise, giving the same relative noise reduction between adjacent nodes. In Section 5 , we compare students trained identically except for the noise schedule: polynomial with ρ = 7 \rho=7 or geometric. Figure 2: Allocation matters most at low budgets. The same untrained AF3 denoiser is evaluated with the default and geometric schedules at matched step budgets and positive endpoints.

Indeed, the final positive interval of the default schedule causes the largest average loss of stereochemically checked lDDT, even though an earlier interval causes a larger final coordinate displacement (Figure 3 ). Coordinate error alone therefore does not explain the damage to molecular geometry. This gives us a reason to redistribute the noise intervals before distillation, as the geometric schedule does. sections.heading: 4.3 Multistep consistency distillation
sections.text: We adapt multistep consistency distillation ( Heek et al., 2024 ) to the variance-exploding EDM coordinates used by AF3 and Boltz-2. The geometric grid divides the trajectory into K K fixed segments, with boundaries b 0 > ⋯ > b K = 0 b_{0}>\cdots>b_{K}=0 . We refine a separate teacher grid during training, keeping these segment boundaries fixed. We sample an adjacent edge using EDM log-normal importance weights, then identify its student segment. DCFold reports instability with conventional consistency training ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , while DeCAF finds poor physical validity with its consistency-distillation baseline ( Scarpellini et al., 2026 ) . Relaxing the one-step requirement shortens the mapping the student must learn. In our setting, multistep distillation works with an aligned coordinate-space loss and ordinary EDM edge sampling, without DCFold’s Temporal Geodesic Matching. sections.heading: 4.4 Physical steering and target-free selection
sections.text: The Boltz-2 students use physical steering during sampling, with strengths approximated from the teacher’s coordinate corrections. A correction c i c_{i} to the denoised estimate changes the next state by α i ​ c i \alpha_{i}c_{i} , where r i = σ i + 1 / σ i r_{i}=\sigma_{i+1}/\sigma_{i} and α i = S ⁡ ( 1 − r i ) (Euler) , α i = 1 − r i S (exponential update) . \alpha_{i}=S(1-r_{i})\quad\text{(Euler)},\qquad\alpha_{i}=1-r_{i}^{S}\quad\text{(exponential update)}. (7) For each potential, we sum correction vectors before taking their RMS and compare transferred corrections in matched log-noise bins. This guides the weights, which we then validate using accuracy and geometry. This steering did not work well for AF3 in our tests. Blitz reranks five candidates without reference structures or further diffusion calls. We prefer its lower geometry-violation rate; Appendix G.3 compares native confidence.

sections.heading: 5 Data and evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate Blitz using AlphaFold3 ( Abramson et al., 2024 ) and Boltz-2 ( Passaro et al., 2025 ) to assess generality across two all-atom structure prediction systems. The schedule improvements in Sections 4.1 – 4.2 also hold for Chai-1 and Protenix ( Chai Discovery et al., 2024 ; ByteDance AML AI4Science Team et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Benchmarks and reporting.
sections.text: We evaluate the Boltz-2 benchmark ( ∼ \sim 2,300 targets), Runs N’ Poses, and Protenix’s 384-target recent-PDB sample ( Passaro et al., 2025 ; Škrinjar et al., 2025 ; ByteDance AML AI4Science Team et al., 2025 ) . Main configurations use three recycles and five candidates. For brevity, the main text focuses on the Boltz-2 benchmark ( ∼ \sim 2,300 targets). Results for Runs N’ Poses and RecentPDB384, including ligand-evaluation coverage limitations, are reported in Appendices D and E .

sections.heading: Accuracy and physical quality.
sections.text: We use OpenStructure ( Biasini et al., 2013 ) to score complex and backbone lDDT, interfaces, ligand placement, and bond, angle, and clash violations. Complex lDDT includes stereochemical checks ( Mariani et al., 2013 ) . Ligand validity is evaluated separately with DeCAF-compatible PoseBusters ( Buttenschoen et al., 2024 ) . Success requires the same primary ligand to pass PB-valid and RMSD < 2 <2 Å in the same candidate. We also report the fraction of targets with geometry defects. sections.heading: 5.2 What does the average hide?
sections.text: The polynomial ( ρ = 7 \rho=7 ) and geometric students use the same training setup, differing only in the noise schedule. They have close average lDDT, but their errors are distributed very differently. Figure 5 compares them on the same targets using the same ranking rule. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and future work
sections.text: This work addresses a central problem in evaluating fast structure prediction: high structural-similarity scores can obscure failures in molecular geometry. We combine a geometric noise schedule with multistep consistency training, physical steering, and reference-free candidate selection. Across AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, this approach retains much of the teachers’ structural accuracy under stereochemically checked evaluation. With the full inference procedure, most predictions from the sixteen-step AF3 student have no counted geometry defects, and fewer predictions are affected than for the corresponding teacher. Its remaining clash burden is concentrated in a relatively small subset of targets. Several accuracy measures also improve over the teacher; our paired comparisons and uncertainty estimates distinguish these gains from differences that remain uncertain. Blitz provides a practical alternative to the expensive diffusion stage in workflows that repeatedly call a structure predictor, including protein design, virtual screening, and antibody candidate evaluation. Our speedup applies to this stage rather than the full prediction pipeline; the trunk remains unchanged and still represents a substantial computational cost. Future work could combine few-step diffusion with methods that reduce trunk computation or strengthen physical constraints during sampling. Our results show that substantial acceleration need not come at the expense of structural accuracy or molecular geometry, provided both are considered in training, inference, and evaluation. Average similarity scores alone cannot establish that quality has been preserved. Evaluation should make clear what is preserved, how often predictions fail, and how severe those failures are. Claims of successful acceleration should account for all three.

sections.heading: Scoring choices.
sections.text: We use OpenStructure’s structural and chemical scores ( Biasini et al., 2013 ; OpenStructure developers, ) , with stereochemical checks enabled for complex lDDT unless marked unchecked ( Mariani et al., 2013 ) . Lai Affiliation: Department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University Affiliation: Institute for Computational and Data Sciences, The Pennsylvania State University Affiliation: Department of Biochemistry, University at Buffalo, State University of New York Abstract Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics. 1 Introduction Diffusion-based atom prediction has been a major breakthrough in the biological sciences, with models such as AlphaFold3 ( Abramson et al., 2024 ) , Boltz-1 and Boltz-2 ( Wohlwend et al., 2024 ; Passaro et al., 2025 ) , Chai-1 ( Chai Discovery et al., 2024 ) , and Protenix ( ByteDance AML AI4Science Team et al., 2025 ) . It builds on progress in protein folding that led CASP organizers to describe AlphaFold2 as a solution to the decades-old folding problem for single protein chains ( Abbass, 2025 ) . However, these models are expensive in pipelines that require tens of thousands of predictions, leading to a growing literature on reducing their cost. These efforts primarily tackle three parts of the pipeline: 1. Reducing the cost of constructing multiple sequence alignments (MSAs). MMseqs2 and ColabFold accelerate sequence search ( Steinegger & Söding, 2017 ; Mirdita et al., 2022 ) , while Kallenborn et al. (2025) move the search onto GPUs. 2. Reducing the number of recycle updates and the computational cost of the Pairformer trunk ( Gong et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . 3. Reducing the cost of the diffusion model itself, which typically uses 200 denoising steps in AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 ( Abramson et al., 2024 ; Passaro et al., 2025 ) . On the model side, these costs have been approached in several ways. Gong et al. (2025) introduced Protenix-Mini, reducing both the cost of the trunk and the number of diffusion sampling steps. Zhang et al. (2026) introduced DCFold, whose Temporal Geodesic Matching schedule pairs diffusion times during consistency training to improve stability. They also apply consistency training to the Pairformer to reduce recycling. Scarpellini et al. (2026) introduced DeCAF, which distills all-atom flow maps in the noise coordinate used by EDM and applies reward-guided search at inference. They report strong results in both protein–ligand pose accuracy and physical validity. However, we show here that differences in scoring conventions and benchmark construction make these algorithms difficult to compare. Claims of preserved quality do not fully hold under our unified evaluation. This is especially important for few-step samplers, where steric clashes, distorted bonds, and invalid bond angles can coexist with high structural similarity scores. Our matched evaluations show that commonly reported accuracy metrics can obscure these flaws when stereochemical checks are omitted (Table 1 and Figure 1 ). To address these gaps in stereochemical quality and structural accuracy, we present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework. We first show that the default polynomial noise schedule of Karras et al. (2022) is ill-suited to the few-step molecular sampling regime studied here, and replace it with a geometric schedule. We then address the remaining accuracy gap with multistep consistency training on this grid, adapting the method of Heek et al. (2024) . The eight-step trajectory also leaves room for inference-time steering, as used in Boltz-2 ( Passaro et al., 2025 ) . We tune the steering strengths for Boltz-2-Blitz and bring its reference-free validity closer to that of its teacher. Finally, we benchmark structural accuracy and stereochemical quality on three popular datasets used in this literature: the Boltz-2 benchmark ( ∼ \sim 2,300 targets), Runs N’ Poses, and RecentPDB384 ( Passaro et al., 2025 ; Škrinjar et al., 2025 ; ByteDance AML AI4Science Team et al., 2025 ) . Among the compared configurations, AF3-Blitz achieves the highest stereochecked complex lDDT on the primary benchmark. Both students retain teacher-level structural accuracy, exceeding their teachers on several reported metrics. We apply the same framework to AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 to show generality across two publicly available diffusion-based structure prediction models. In summary, our core contributions are: 1. A diagnosis. We show that prevailing scoring and benchmark conventions systematically mask the geometric failures of few-step structure predictors, and we expose these failures under matched evaluation. 2. A method. We introduce Blitz, which pairs a geometric noise schedule and multistep consistency training with inference-time physical controls to reach teacher-level structural accuracy in eight sampling steps, a 25 × 25\times reduction in sampling steps for both AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2. 3. A protocol. We establish a standardized, multi-metric evaluation across three benchmarks spanning structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemistry, designed to surface the failure modes that single-metric reporting hides. 2 Background: diffusion and consistency distillation Diffusion in AlphaFold3. AF3 adopts the EDM formulation and polynomial noise schedule of Karras et al. (2022) for all-atom structure prediction ( Abramson et al., 2024 , Supplementary Information, Sections 3.7–3.7.1) . Its diffusion module is a non-equivariant transformer conditioned on the single and pair representations from the trunk. Let x 0 ∈ ℝ N × 3 x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} contain the resolved atomic coordinates and c c the molecular features and trunk conditioning. In these variance-exploding coordinates, a training input is x σ = x 0 + σ ​ ϵ , ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) . x_{\sigma}=x_{0}+\sigma\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). Consistency models learn to map points on the same probability-flow trajectory to its low-noise endpoint ( Song et al., 2023 ) . For two states x s , x t x_{s},x_{t} on that trajectory, the desired property is f θ ​ ( x s , s ) = f θ ​ ( x t , t ) f_{\theta}(x_{s},s)=f_{\theta}(x_{t},t) , with the boundary condition f θ ​ ( x ε , ε ) = x ε f_{\theta}(x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon)=x_{\varepsilon} at a small positive endpoint ε \varepsilon . In consistency distillation, a frozen diffusion teacher takes a numerical step to form a pair of nearby states. Training brings their student predictions together, stopping gradients through the target branch. Consistency training instead forms pairs directly from noised data, without a pretrained teacher ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2024 ) . Multistep consistency models. Heek et al. (2024) unify TRACT ( Berthelot et al., 2023 ) and consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) by dividing the trajectory into fixed segments. A shared model maps each point to the lower boundary of its segment. Generation traverses the segments in order, using one evaluation per segment. The prediction in Figure 1 a has severe overlap between its protein chains. Despite having recognizable individual folds, this arrangement is sterically implausible; however, it still scores well on unchecked lDDT. Its Boltz-1x teacher, shown in Figure 1 b, retains recognizable folds without this severe overlap; this raises an important question: what must accelerated structure prediction preserve when we remove these denoising steps? This is particularly important when there is a claim that a faster sampler preserves accuracy. Unchecked lDDT measures how well local interatomic distances are preserved from the reference. However, this local fold preservation can coexist with severe clashes and violations of bond lengths and angles. The original lDDT authors anticipated this distinction and provided optional stereochemical checks to account for these violations ( Mariani et al., 2013 ) . PoseBusters showed that agreement with an experimental ligand pose does not necessarily establish physical plausibility ( Buttenschoen et al., 2024 ) . However, evaluations like those done by DCFold report only RMSD thresholds on the PoseBusters benchmark without reporting PB-validity, leaving the failure mode that motivated those checks unexamined ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . This concern also applies to cofolding. AlphaFold3 documents overlapping chains ( Abramson et al., 2024 ) , and DeCAF reports ligand validity alongside pose accuracy ( Scarpellini et al., 2026 ) . Following the deterministic analysis of Karras et al. (2022) , we hold the pretrained AF3 denoiser and solver fixed and replace the default Karras schedule with a geometric schedule. Stereochemically checked lDDT improves while bond violations and clashes decrease, as shown in Figure 2 . Critically, the improvement is largest at the smallest step budgets. The fold alone does not capture the difference in molecular geometry. DeCAF default uses the released ten-step sampler ( γ = 1 \gamma=1 ); its SDE variant uses γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 without guidance. DeCAF FK uses four particles and ten steps, requiring 40 denoiser evaluations per retained pose. FK steering improves ligand validity, while substantial protein-geometry violations remain. 5.2 What does the average hide? The polynomial ( ρ = 7 \rho=7 ) and geometric students use the same training setup, differing only in the noise schedule. They have close average lDDT, but their errors are distributed very differently. Figure 5 compares them on the same targets using the same ranking rule. Most predictions from the geometric student avoid counted geometry violations altogether. The ρ = 7 \rho=7 student’s defects are spread across many more targets, even though the mean clash counts are close. Indeed, an average alone misses both parts of this result: how often a structure is damaged and how badly it is damaged when it fails. The paired accuracy changes and the violation tail show the remaining trade-off. Appendices F and G examine how target size and individual outliers affect these results. B–C: defect frequency and violation-count tails on matched Boltz-2 benchmark targets. A uses a signed-log change axis; C uses log-scaled counts and percentages, with a linear region near zero count. Zero counted violations does not imply full chemical validity. 6 Conclusion and future work This work addresses a central problem in evaluating fast structure prediction: high structural-similarity scores can obscure failures in molecular geometry. We combine a geometric noise schedule with multistep consistency training, physical steering, and reference-free candidate selection. Across AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, this approach retains much of the teachers’ structural accuracy under stereochemically checked evaluation. With the full inference procedure, most predictions from the sixteen-step AF3 student have no counted geometry defects, and fewer predictions are affected than for the corresponding teacher. Its remaining clash burden is concentrated in a relatively small subset of targets. Several accuracy measures also improve over the teacher; our paired comparisons and uncertainty estimates distinguish these gains from differences that remain uncertain. Blitz provides a practical alternative to the expensive diffusion stage in workflows that repeatedly call a structure predictor, including protein design, virtual screening, and antibody candidate evaluation. Our speedup applies to this stage rather than the full prediction pipeline; the trunk remains unchanged and still represents a substantial computational cost. Future work could combine few-step diffusion with methods that reduce trunk computation or strengthen physical constraints during sampling. Our results show that substantial acceleration need not come at the expense of structural accuracy or molecular geometry, provided both are considered in training, inference, and evaluation. Average similarity scores alone cannot establish that quality has been preserved. Evaluation should make clear what is preserved, how often predictions fail, and how severe those failures are.
